svg.title: Same size, different shape
svg.desc: Two models with the same number of parameters but different shapes. Each is drawn as a small neural network, with circles for neurons and lines for weights. Model A is wide and shallow: few, tall columns of neurons, standing for 24 layers that are 1,856 numbers wide. Model B is narrow and deep: more, shorter columns, standing for 48 layers that are 1,312 numbers wide. Each comes to about 0.99 billion parameters. After training on the same data, both reach almost the same quality. In scaling-law studies (Kaplan et al., 2020), models of the same size with very different shapes ended up within a few percent of each other. Only extreme shapes hurt: for example 2 layers with d = 6,450 is also about 1 billion parameters, but has too few layers to build up meaning. Quality bars are illustrative.
svg.text: Two ways to spend about 1 billion parameters. Circles are neurons, lines are weights. Columns show depth, column height shows width.
AFTER TRAINING ON THE SAME DATA

g.text: models of the same size with very different
shapes ended up within a few percent of
each other. Total size and data matter most.
Same size again, but too few layers to build
up meaning. The opposite extreme, tiny
vectors and hundreds of layers, squeezes
too much into each token's vector.

svg.text: Scaled-down sketch: both drawn at 1/8 of their real depth, widths kept in the same ratio. Parameter counts leave out the embedding table. Quality bars are illustrative.
